readings.c1s1:
all members of a particular race, or of the human race in general, as regards each other.
{{smaller block|Jacob told Rachel that he was her father’s ''brother'' [that is, his uncle Laban’s].
{{right|Gen. xxix. 12.}}
Let us send abroad unto our ''brethren'' everywhere, that are left in all the land of Israel.
{{right|1 Chron. xiii. 2.}}
<poem>
Of whom such massacre
Make they, but of their ''brethren''; men of men?
</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 680.}}}}
'''3.''' One of two or more men closely united without regard to personal kinship, as by a common interest; an associate; one of the same rank, profession, occupation, or belief, especially in law, religion, or organized charity.
{{smaller block|<poem>
We few, we happy few, we band of ''brothers'';
For he to-day that sheds his blood with me
Shall be my ''brother''.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iv. 3.}}}}
'''4.''' Specifically, as a translation of ''friar'', a member of a mendicant order.
{{smaller block|<poem>
Going to find a barefoot ''brother'' out,
One of our order.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., v. 2.}}}}
'''5.''' In the plural form ''brethren'', the designation of several Christian organizations, derived from the fact that the title was used by the primitive Christians in speaking of themselves; specifically, a sect of German Baptists, more popularly known as ''Dunkers''.—'''6.''' A member of a religious congregation whose members do not receive the priesthood, but devote themselves to teaching or good works; also, a lay member of a community having priests.—'''7.''' Figuratively, one who resembles another in manners or disposition.
{{smaller block|He also that is slothful in his work is ''brother'' to him}}

'''brotherhead†''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-hed), ''n.'' [< ME. ''brotherhed'', var. of ''brotherhod''.] See ''brotherhood''.

'''brotherhood''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-hu̇d), ''n.'' [< ME. ''brotherhod'' (usually ''brotherhed'', E. ''brotherhead''); < ''brother'' + ''-hood''.] '''1.''' The fact or condition of being a brother.
{{smaller block|<poem>My brother kill’d no man, his fault was thought,
And yet his punishment was bitter death.
Who sued to me for him? . . .
Who spoke of ''brotherhood?''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., ii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' The quality of being brotherly.
{{smaller block|<poem>And friendship shall combine, and ''brotherhood''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., ii. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' An association of men for any purpose; a fraternity.
{{smaller block|The church was a ''brotherhood;'' no other relation so aptly distinguished the spirit of union and self-sacrifice which it was designed should belong to it.
{{right|''G. P. Fisher'', Begin. of Christianity, p. 549.}}}}
'''4.''' A class of individuals of the same kind, profession, or occupation.
{{smaller block|The ''brotherhood'' of Christendom.
{{right|''Burke'', A Regicide Peace, ii.}}
<poem>The gloom
Spread by a ''brotherhood'' of lofty elms.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Excursion, i.}}}}

'''brother-in-law''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-in-lâ″), ''n.'' [< ME. ''brother in lawe'', ''brodyr yn lawe'', etc., after OF. ''frere en lay'' [''loi''], ML. ''frater in lege''.] The brother of one’s husband or wife; also, one’s sister’s husband. {{smaller|For some purposes, but not all, the legal incidents of the affinity cease on the death of the one whose marriage formed the tie.}}

'''brotherless''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-les), ''a.'' [< ME. *''brotherles'', < AS. ''brōthorleás'': see ''brother'' and ''-less''.] Without a brother.

'''brotherliness''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-li-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being brotherly.

'''brother-love†''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-luv), ''n.'' Brotherly affection. ''Shak.''

'''brotherly''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-li), ''a.'' [< ME. *''brotherly'', < AS. ''brōthorlīc'': see ''brother'' and ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.] Pertaining to brothers; such as is natural for brothers; becoming brothers; kind; affectionate: as, ''brotherly'' love. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''Brotherly, Fraternal.'' The former of these words expresses the more affection; the latter is often more formal or official.}}
{{smaller block|Be kindly affectioned one to another with ''brotherly'' love.
{{right|Rom. xii. 10.}}
<poem>Who, not content
With fair equality, ''fraternal'' state,
Will arrogate dominion undeserved
Over his brethren.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 26.}}}}

'''brotherly†''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-li), ''adv.'' After the manner of a brother; kindly; affectionately.
{{smaller block|With these principles who knows but that at length he might have come to take the Covenant, as others, whom they ''Brotherly'' admitt, have don before him.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, ix.}}}}

'''brotherwort''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-wėrt), ''n.'' An old name for the creeping thyme, ''Thymus Serpyllum.''

'''brothly†''', ''adv.'' See ''brathly''.

'''brothy†''', ''a.'' [ME.; origin obscure.] Shaggy; stiff.
{{smaller block|His berde was ''brothy'' and blake, that tille his brest rechede.

'''brott''' (brot), ''n.'' [Appar. < Icel. ''brot'', a broken piece, a fragment (cf. ''broti'', trees felled and left

lying), < ''brjōta'' (= AS. ''breótan'', pp. ''broten''), break: see ''brit''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''brot-ground'', ''brotus''.] '''1.''' Shaken corn. ''Brockett.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''2.''' ''pl.'' Fragments; droppings; leavings. [Prov. Eng.]

'''Brotula''' (brot′ū-lä̤), ''n.'' [NL.] A genus of fishes, typical of the family ''Brotulidæ'', now restricted
[[FIGURE]]

to ''B. barbata'', a species found in the Caribbean sea.

'''brotulid''' (brot′ū-lid), ''n.'' A fish of the family ''Brotulidæ''. Also called ''brotuloid''.

'''Brotulidæ''' (bro-tū′li-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Brotula'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of teleocephalous fishes, typified by the genus ''Brotula'', having various limits in different systems. {{smaller|Made by Gill a family of ''Ophidioidea'', with jugular ventrals reduced to one or two rays, and the anus in the anterior half of the length.}}

'''Brotulina''' (brot-ū-lī′nä̤), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Brotula'' + ''-ina''.] In Günther’s system of classification, the first group of ''Ophidiidæ'', having ventral fins developed and attached to the humeral arch.

'''Brotulinæ''' (brot-ụ̄-lī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Brotula'' + ''-inæ''.] A subfamily of brotuloid fishes, typified by the genus ''Brotula'', to which different limits have been assigned.

'''brotuline''' (brot′ụ̄-lin), ''n.'' and ''a.'' '''I.''' ''n.'' A fish of the subfamily ''Brotulinæ''.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to or having the characters of the ''Brotulinæ'' or ''Brotulidæ''.

'''brotuloid''' (brot′ụ̄-loid), ''n.'' and ''a.'' '''I.''' ''n.'' Same as ''brotulid''.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to or having the characters of the ''Brotulidæ''.

'''brotulophidid''' (brot-ụ̄-lof′i-did), ''n.'' A fish of the family ''Brotulophididæ''.

'''Brotulophididæ''' (brot″ụ̄-lọ̄-fid′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Brotulophis'' (''-phid-'') + ''-idæ''.] A family of ''Ophidioidea'', represented by the genus ''Brotulophis'', and including ophidioids with subbrachial (or thoracic) ventrals reduced to simple filaments, and the anus in the anterior half of the length.

'''Brotulophis''' (bro-tū′lọ̄-fis), ''n.'' [NL., < ''Brotula'' + Gr. ὄφις, a serpent.] The typical genus of the family ''Brotulophididæ'', having the aspect of ''Brotula'', but still more elongate and snakelike, whence the name.

'''brotus''' (brô′tus), ''n.'' [Cf. E. dial. ''brotts'', fragments, leavings, droppings, ult. < AS. ''breótan'' (pp. ''broten''), break: see ''brit''<sup>1</sup>, ''brott''.] Something added gratuitously; an additional number or quantity thrown in: same as ''lagniappe'': used by negroes and others about Charleston, South Carolina.

''brouden'', ''browden'', etc., also ''broiden'', etc., variants of ''braiden'', etc., braid: see ''braid''1, and cf. ''broid'', ''broider''.] '''1.''' To braid. {{smaller block|Hire yolwe heer was ''browded'' [var. ''broyded'', ''breided''] in a tresse,
Byhynde hire bak, a yerde long I gesse. {{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 191.}}}} '''2.''' To embroider. {{smaller block|Whit was hire smok, and ''browdid'' al byfore And eek behind on hire coler aboute Of cole-blak silk. {{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 52.}}}} '''brouder†''', '''browder†''', ''v. t.'' Variants of ''broider''. {{smaller block|Where’er you spy This ''browdered'' belt with characters, ’tis I. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Sad Shepherd, ii. 1.}}}} '''broudery†''', ''n.'' A variant of ''broidery''. '''brouding†''', '''browding†''', ''n.'' Embroidery. {{smaller block|Harness . . . wrought so weel Of goldsmithrye, of ''browding'', and of steel. {{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1640.}}}} '''brouette''' (brö-et′), ''n.'' [F., a wheelbarrow, also, in contempt, a carriage, formerly also a sedan chair; ult. < LL. ''birota'': see ''barouche''.] A small two-wheeled carriage. '''brough'''1 (broċh), ''n.'' [Also ''brugh'', a var. of ''burgh'', ''burch'', for ''borough'': see ''borough''1.] '''1.''' A borough.—'''2.''' A fortified place. Compare ''brough''2. [Scotch in both senses.] '''brough'''2 (broċh), ''n.'' [Also ''brugh'', ''brogh'', ''broch'', and ''burg'', ''burrow''; supposed to be a particular use of ''brough''1, ''burg'', for ''borough''1, a fortified
readings.c3s3:
place; but in the sense of ‘circle,’ ‘halo,’ cf. ''burrow''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'', 4.] '''1.''' An ancient circular building or round tower such as exist in Scotland and the adjacent islands. {{smaller|The Burg of Mousa is a circular building 41 feet high; its walls, which are double, with a vacant space between them, diminish from 14 feet in width at the base to 8 feet at the summit, and inclose a central area; the door is 7 feet high. These structures are older than the Scandinavian invasions, and probably date almost from the bronze age.}} '''2.''' An encampment of a circular form; a ring fort. Also called ''Pecht’s'' [''Pict’s''] ''house'' or ''Pecht’s castle.''—'''3.''' In the game of curling, one of the two circles drawn around the tee.—'''4.''' A hazy circle around the sun or moon, considered as a presage of a change of weather. [Scotch in all senses.]

'''brough<sup>3</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''brow.''

'''brougham''' (brö′am or bröm), ''n.'' [After the first Lord ''Brougham.''] A four-wheeled close
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{smaller|Brougham.}}}}
carriage, with one or two horses, and adapted to carry either two or four persons.

'''brought''' (brôt). Preterit and past participle of ''bring.''

'''brouillerie†''', ''n.'' See ''broilery.''

'''brouk†''', ''v. t.'' An older form of ''brook''<sup>2</sup>.

'''brouse†''', ''v.'' See ''bruise.''

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|brother|696|brouse}}</noinclude>all members of a particular race, or of the human race in general, as regards each other.
{{smaller block|Jacob told Rachel that he was her father’s ''brother'' [that is, his uncle Laban’s].
{{right|Gen. xxix. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|Let us send abroad unto our ''brethren'' everywhere, that are left in all the land of Israel.
{{right|1 Chron. xiii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
Of whom such massacre
Make they, but of their ''brethren''; men of men?
</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 680.}}}}
'''3.''' One of two or more men closely united without regard to personal kinship, as by a common interest; an associate; one of the same rank, profession, occupation, or belief, especially in law, religion, or organized charity.
{{smaller block|<poem>
We few, we happy few, we band of ''brothers'';
For he to-day that sheds his blood with me
Shall be my ''brother''.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iv. 3.}}}}
'''4.''' Specifically, as a translation of ''friar'', a member of a mendicant order.
{{smaller block|<poem>
Going to find a barefoot ''brother'' out,
One of our order.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., v. 2.}}}}
'''5.''' In the plural form ''brethren'', the designation of several Christian organizations, derived from the fact that the title was used by the primitive Christians in speaking of themselves; specifically, a sect of German Baptists, more popularly known as ''Dunkers''.—'''6.''' A member of a religious congregation whose members do not receive the priesthood, but devote themselves to teaching or good works; also, a lay member of a community having priests.—'''7.''' Figuratively, one who resembles another in manners or disposition.
{{smaller block|He also that is slothful in his work is ''brother'' to him that is a great waster.{{right|Prov. xviii. 9.}}}}

Often abbreviated ''bro.'', plural ''bros.''

{{smaller|[The plural form ''brethren'' is not now used in the sense of male children of the same parents, but only in the wider meanings of the word ''brother''.]—'''Amyclæan brothers.''' See ''Amyclæan''.—'''Apostolic Brethren.''' See ''apostolic'', ''n.'', 1 (''c''), and ''Apostoline''.—'''Arval Brethren''' or '''Brothers.''' See ''arval''<sup>2</sup>.—'''Attidian Brethren.''' See ''Attidian''.—'''Bohemian Brethren.''' See ''Bohemian''.—'''Brethren and Clerks of the Common Life,''' a monastic fraternity, clerical and lay, originating in the Netherlands about 1376, devoted to education and labor, and not bound by perpetual vows. Thomas à Kempis belonged to it. It spread widely, but became extinct in the seventeenth century. There was a female branch of the order.—'''Brethren of Chelcic,''' followers of Peter Chelczicky, a Bohemian reformer of the fifteenth century. They were organized into a separate community in 1457, and soon became known as ''Bohemian Brethren''.—'''Brethren of the Christian Schools,''' a Roman Catholic order, consisting chiefly of lay men, devoted to the education of the poor, founded in France in 1679, and now numerous in various parts of the world.—'''Brethren of the Community,''' one of the two parties into which the Franciscans were divided in the beginning of the fourteenth century.—'''Brethren of the Free Spirit,''' a sect which arose in the thirteenth century, pantheistic in doctrine, perfectionists in principle, and enthusiasts in practice.—'''Brethren of the Holy Spirit,''' or '''Brethren of the Redemption of Captives,''' an order of monks in the twelfth century who devoted themselves to the redemption of captives from the Mohammedans.—'''Brothers of Charity.''' See ''charity''.—'''Christian Brothers.''' See ''Christian''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Elder Brethren,''' the masters of Trinity House, London, the corporation charged with the regulation and management of the lighthouses and buoys on the shores and rivers of England, with the licensing of pilots, and with a general supervision over the lighthouse boards of Scotland and Ireland, called respectively the Commissioners of Northern Lights and the Ballast Board of Dublin.—'''Exclusive Brethren.''' See ''Plymouth Brethren'', below.—'''Full brothers.''' See ''full.''—'''Plymouth Brethren, Plymouthites,''' a sect of Christians which first attracted notice at Plymouth, England, in 1830, but has since extended over Great Britain, the United States, and among the Protestants of France, Switzerland, Italy, etc. They recognize all as brethren who believe in Christ and the Holy Spirit as his vicar, but they have no formal creed, ecclesiastical organization, or official ministry, which they condemn as the causes of sectarian divisions. Also called ''Darbyites'', after Mr. Darby, originally a barrister, subsequently a clergyman of the Church of England, and thereafter an evangelist not connected with any church, to whose efforts their origin and the diffusion of their principles are to be ascribed. In a narrower sense the Darbyites are a branch of the Plymouth Brethren, entitled ''Exclusive Brethren'', on account of the strictness of their views and the exclusiveness of their communion.—'''United Brethren,''' or '''Unity of Brethren''' (''Unitas Fratrum''), the official designation of the Bohemian Brethren and of their successors the Moravian Brethren, or Moravians.}}

'''brother''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''a.'' Bearing a fraternal relation in a general sense; of the character of a brother: as, a ''brother'' man or magistrate.
{{smaller block|It was then removed and planted in a remote place close to a ''brother'' long-style plant.
{{right|''Darwin.''}}}}

'''brother''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''brother'', ''n.'']   '''1.''' To consider or treat as a brother; address as a brother.—'''2.''' To relate as brothers; make kin.
{{smaller block|One Die, one Mintage, one Humanity; every man the kinsman of every other; mankind ''brothered'' in the one mould of the Creative Word.
{{right|''G. D. Boardman'', Creative Week, p. 196.}}}}

'''brother-german''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-jėr′man), ''n.''   [< ''brother'' + ''german''<sup>1</sup>; cf. Sp. ''hermano'', a brother, under ''brother''.]   A brother on both the father’s and the mother’s side; a full brother.

'''brotherhead†''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-hed), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brotherhed'', var. of ''brotherhod''.]   See ''brotherhood''.

{{smaller block|<poem>My brother kill’d no man, his fault was thought,
And yet his punishment was bitter death.
Who sued to me for him? . . .
Who spoke of ''brotherhood?''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., ii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' The quality of being brotherly.
{{smaller block|<poem>And friendship shall combine, and ''brotherhood''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., ii. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' An association of men for any purpose; a fraternity.
{{smaller block|The church was a ''brotherhood;'' no other relation so aptly distinguished the spirit of union and self-sacrifice which it was designed should belong to it.
{{right|''G. P. Fisher'', Begin. of Christianity, p. 549.}}}}
'''4.''' A class of individuals of the same kind, profession, or occupation.
{{smaller block|The ''brotherhood'' of Christendom.
{{right|''Burke'', A Regicide Peace, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The gloom
Spread by a ''brotherhood'' of lofty elms.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Excursion, i.}}}}

''frater in lege''.]   The brother of one’s husband or wife; also, one’s sister’s husband. {{smaller|For some purposes, but not all, the legal incidents of the affinity cease on the death of the one whose marriage formed the tie.}}

'''brotherly''' (bruᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-li), ''a.''   [< ME. *''brotherly'', < AS. ''brōthorlīc'': see ''brother'' and ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   Pertaining to brothers; such as is natural for brothers; becoming brothers; kind; affectionate: as, ''brotherly'' love. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''Brotherly, Fraternal.'' The former of these words expresses the more affection; the latter is often more formal or official.}}
{{smaller block|Be kindly affectioned one to another with ''brotherly'' love.
{{right|Rom. xii. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Who, not content
With fair equality, ''fraternal'' state,
Will arrogate dominion undeserved

{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 26.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Whit was hire smok, and ''browdid'' al byfore

'''brouder†''', '''browder†''', ''v. t.'' Variants of ''broider''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Where’er you spy
This ''browdered'' belt with characters, ’tis I.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sad Shepherd, ii. 1.}}}}

'''broudery†''', ''n.'' A variant of ''broidery''.

'''brouding†''', '''browding†''', ''n.'' Embroidery.
{{smaller block|<poem>Harness . . . wrought so weel
Of goldsmithrye, of ''browding'', and of steel.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1640.}}}}

'''brouette''' (brö-et′), ''n.''   [F., a wheelbarrow, also, in contempt, a carriage, formerly also a sedan chair; ult. < LL. ''birota'': see ''barouche''.]   A small two-wheeled carriage.

'''brough'''<sup>1</sup> (broċh), ''n.''   [Also ''brugh'', a var. of ''burgh'', ''burch'', for ''borough'': see ''borough''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A borough.—'''2.''' A fortified place. Compare ''brough''<sup>2</sup>. [Scotch in both senses.]

'''brough'''<sup>2</sup> (broċh), ''n.''   [Also ''brugh'', ''brogh'', ''broch'', and ''burg'', ''burrow''; supposed to be a particular use of ''brough''<sup>1</sup>, ''burg'', for ''borough''<sup>1</sup>, a fortified place; but in the sense of ‘circle,’ ‘halo,’ cf. ''burrow''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'', 4.]   '''1.''' An ancient circular building or round tower such as exist in Scotland and the adjacent islands. {{smaller|The Burg of Mousa is a circular building 41 feet high; its walls, which are double, with a vacant space between them, diminish from 14 feet in width at the base to 8 feet at the summit, and inclose a central area; the door is 7 feet high. These structures are older than the Scandinavian invasions, and probably date almost from the bronze age.}} '''2.''' An encampment of a circular form; a ring fort. Also called ''Pecht’s'' [''Pict’s''] ''house'' or ''Pecht’s castle.''—'''3.''' In the game of curling, one of the two circles drawn around the tee.—'''4.''' A hazy circle around the sun or moon, considered as a presage of a change of weather. [Scotch in all senses.]

'''brough<sup>3</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''brow.''

'''brougham''' (brö′am or bröm), ''n.''   [After the first Lord ''Brougham.'']   A four-wheeled close {{img float|file=century v01 p0722 c3f1.png|width=222px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Brougham.}}}} carriage, with one or two horses, and adapted to carry either two or four persons.

'''brought''' (brôt). Preterit and past participle of ''bring.''

'''brouillerie†''', ''n.'' See ''broilery.''

'''brouk†''', ''v. t.'' An older form of ''brook''<sup>2</sup>.

'''brouse†''', ''v.'' See ''bruise.''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
